title: Malfouf
subtitle: Lebanese stuffed cabbage rolls in tomato and lemon broth
excerpt: Malfouf are Lebanese stuffed cabbage rolls: blanched white cabbage leaves wrapped around a filling of lamb mince, rice, and warm spices, simmered in a sharp, lemony tomato broth until the filling is cooked through and the cabbage very tender.
sourceNotes: Claudia Roden, A Book of Middle Eastern Food (1968). Stuffed cabbage rolls documented across Lebanon, Syria, and Egypt. Anissa Helou, Lebanese Cuisine (1994). Malfouf described with the sharp lemon broth as the defining feature of the Lebanese version.

recipe.freezeNotes: Cool completely, then freeze in portions with their broth. Reheat gently on the hob.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Roll the cabbage up to a day ahead and refrigerate. Cook in the broth when ready.

content.text: Malfouf are Lebanese cabbage rolls stuffed with a raw lamb and rice mixture, simmered in a broth sharpened with lemon juice and crushed garlic. The lemon and garlic broth is what distinguishes the Lebanese version from other stuffed cabbage traditions; the sharp, aromatic liquid penetrates the rolls during the long, slow cook. Serve in shallow bowls with some broth spooned over and good bread alongside.

Bring a large pot of water to the boil. Core the {{cabbage-white}} from the base. Lower the whole head into the boiling water for three to four minutes, then remove and peel off the softened outer leaves. Return to the water and repeat until you have 16 to 20 usable leaves. Pat them dry.
Trim any thick rib from the base of each leaf so it rolls more easily.
In a bowl, mix {{lamb-mince}} with {{long-grain-rice}} and grated {{onion}}. Add {{allspice}}, {{cinnamon-ground}}, {{sea-salt-fine}}, and {{black-pepper}}. Mix until combined.
Place a heaped tablespoon of filling near the stem end of each leaf. Fold the sides in and roll up firmly from the stem end. The rolls should be snug but not tight.
Line the base of a large heavy saucepan with any broken or spare cabbage leaves. Pack the rolls in snug layers, seam side down.

Mix {{tinned-tomatoes}}, {{tomato-puree}}, lemon juice from {{lemon}}, crushed {{garlic}}, {{sea-salt-fine}}, and 300 ml of water together. Pour over the rolls. The liquid should just cover the top layer.

Bring to the boil, cover, and simmer on a low heat for 50 to 60 minutes until the rice filling is cooked through and the cabbage is very tender. Check occasionally and add a splash of water if needed.

items.symptom: The rolls have opened during cooking
items.cause: Not rolled tightly enough or placed seam side up
items.fix: Pack the rolls tightly in the pot, seam side down. They support each other and stay closed during the long braise.

items.symptom: The filling is still raw after an hour
items.cause: Not enough liquid, or the rolls were packed too tightly
items.fix: Add boiling water and increase the heat slightly. The steam needs to penetrate the rolls throughout the cook.

items.symptom: The broth tastes too sharp from the lemon
items.cause: Too much lemon juice for the quantity of liquid
items.fix: Add the lemon juice in stages, tasting as you go. The sharpness is characteristic but should not be overwhelming.

items.symptom: The cabbage leaves tear when rolling
items.cause: Not blanched long enough to soften fully
items.fix: Return the cabbage to the boiling water for another two minutes. The leaves should be pliable, not stiff.

content.text: Malfouf means wrapped in Arabic. Stuffed cabbage rolls are a classic of Lebanese and Syrian home cooking, made in winter when fresh vine leaves are not available as a wrapper. Stuffed vegetables are common across the eastern Mediterranean and Middle East, and the cabbage roll version also appears in Turkish, Greek, and Polish cooking. The Lebanese version uses a lot of lemon and garlic in the cooking liquid, giving the rolls a bright, sharp taste. In some households, the dish is inverted onto a plate and served with its broth.
